publisher: UTokyo College of Design, University of Tokyo
claim: The University of Tokyo opens a new English-taught undergraduate faculty, the UTokyo College of Design, in September 2027. It takes 100 students on a five-year integrated bachelor's and master's programme through two routes, and Route B is for applicants using international qualifications, the International Baccalaureate Diploma named first among them. Applications run from 15 October 2026 at 09:00 to 5 November 2026 at 17:00 JST.
excerpt: 100 Students (Route A: 50 students, Route B: 50 students) […] Route A is for people who wish to use the Japanese "Common Test for University Admissions" and Route B is for people who wish to use other standardized tests and qualifications designated by the University of Tokyo (e.g. International Baccalaureate, International A-Levels, or other tests that are standard in your country). There are no nationality restrictions for either route. […] International Baccalaureate Diploma (IB), Abitur, Baccalauréat, GCE A-level, International A-level, European Baccalaureate […] Application Period: October 15, 2026, 9:00 AM – November 5, 2026, 5:00 PM (JST) […] First screening results: December 22, 2026 (Route B) […] Final decisions: February 20, 2027 […] All courses are taught in English
interpretation: This is the far more useful half of the University of Tokyo story and it replaces the flat statement that Todai has closed. PEAK ended and a larger, differently shaped English-taught route opened in its place: a whole new faculty, the university's first in about seventy years, on a September intake deliberately chosen to match Europe and North America, with half its places reserved for the international route. For an IB student in Denmark the consequential detail is the date — applications close on 5 November 2026, six weeks after this was written, with the Route B result on 22 December 2026 and the final decision on 20 February 2027. It is the earliest deadline of any Japanese route recorded here, and it is decided entirely on predicted grades. Note also that this is a five-year integrated programme ending at master's level, not a three- or four-year bachelor's; a student comparing it with a Dutch bachelor is not comparing like with like.

claim: Keio's PEARL economics degree admits about 100 students for entry on 22 September 2027 through three separate application periods, the last of which closes on 7 April 2027, and it accepts an IB Diploma or predicted IB grades.
excerpt: Period I: 10:00 a.m. on October 21, 2026 - 3:00 p.m. on December 2, 2026 (JST), results 10:00 a.m. on January 25, 2027 (JST). Period II: 10:00 a.m. on December 4, 2026 - 3:00 p.m. on January 27, 2027 (JST), results 10:00 a.m. on March 4, 2027 (JST). Period III: 10:00 a.m. on February 24, 2027 - 3:00 p.m. on April 7, 2027 (JST), results 10:00 a.m. on May 24, 2027 (JST). […] Entry: September 22, 2027 […] International Baccalaureate (IB) Diploma (or predicted grades) […] TOEFL iBT® scores […] IELTS Academic Module scores
interpretation: The friendliest Japanese calendar we found for an IB candidate, and the reason is Period III. It closes on 7 April 2027, by which point a May 2027 candidate's predicted grades are settled and their mock results exist, and it announces on 24 May — still before the diploma, but after the exams. Keio also says in as many words that predicted grades are acceptable, which most Japanese programmes leave to inference. The trade is that the three periods share one quota of about 100 places, so a later period is competing for what the earlier ones did not take. Applying in Period I is the stronger position; applying in Period III is the one that fits the Danish school year.

publisher: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), Japan
claim: The MEXT undergraduate scholarship on the Embassy Recommendation runs for five years from April 2027 to March 2032, beginning with one year of preparatory education in Japanese. It pays 117,000 yen a month, waives entrance examination, matriculation and tuition fees and provides an economy air ticket. Applicants must be born on or after 2 April 2002 and have completed twelve years of schooling by March 2027, and in principle must arrive in Japan between 1 and 7 April 2027.
excerpt: Age: Applicants, in principle, must have been born on or after April 2, 2002. […] Academic Background: ① Applicants who have completed 12 years of schooling in countries other than Japan. (Applicants who will meet the above condition by March 2027 are eligible. However, applicants wishing to enroll from the autumn term through direct placement must be expected to complete 12 years of schooling by August 2027.) […] Arrival in Japan: In principle, applicants must be able to arrive in Japan between April 1, 2027, and April 7, 2027. […] The scholarship period will last for five years from April 2027 to March 2032, including one-year preparatory education in the Japanese language and other subjects […] Allowance: 117,000 yen per month […] Education Fees: Fees for the entrance examination, matriculation, and tuition at universities will be waived. […] All classes will be given in the Japanese language (except where a grantee is directly placed at a university which requires no Japanese language ability).
interpretation: The correction this makes is about what MEXT actually is. The old record described it as a route into Japan's English-taught degrees; the guidelines say the opposite — a preparatory year in Japanese, then a university course taught in Japanese, with English-medium study available only through 'direct placement', which MEXT decides and which is the exception rather than the norm. The second correction is the date. This is the 2027 round, applied for through the embassy in the spring of 2026, arriving April 2027, and it is closed. A candidate finishing the IB in May 2027 would meet neither the March 2027 completion condition nor the 1–7 April 2027 arrival window, so their round is 2028 — applied for in the spring of 2027, arriving April 2028. Note the exception in condition ①, which is the one an autumn-term applicant needs: completion by August rather than March, but only for direct placement.

publisher: Ministry of Education, Culture, Sports, Science and Technology (MEXT), Japan
claim: MEXT recruits embassy-recommended undergraduate scholars between April and May of the year before arrival, with first screening by the embassy or consulate between May and August; each country's exact schedule is set by its Japanese diplomatic mission.
excerpt: Recruitment for those arriving in Japan next April is made between April and May of the previous year. First screening is conducted between May and August by the Japanese Embassies or Consulates General. […] As the application process and specific schedule differ according to the country of your nationality, please inquire the Japanese Embassy or Consulate General in your country for details.
interpretation: This is the sentence that fixes a dating error this repository was carrying: a record written in September 2026 told students to contact the Embassy of Japan in Denmark 'in early 2026', which was already in the past when it was written. The rule is relative, not absolute — April and May of the year before arrival — so for an April 2028 arrival the window is April and May 2027, which is exactly when an IB candidate in Denmark is sitting their examinations. That collision is worth saying out loud: the MEXT application and the IB exam session fall in the same eight weeks, and the paperwork includes a health certificate and a recommendation letter that cannot be produced in a hurry. MEXT also says plainly that the exact dates are the embassy's to set, so the national page can never be the last word.

claim: Japan admits international students to five kinds of higher education institution — colleges of technology, specialized training colleges on post-secondary courses, junior colleges, universities and graduate schools. Most institutions run an academic year from April to March and admit in April, though some operate an autumn admission system.
excerpt: there are 5 types of higher education institutions that international students can be admitted to, which are 1) colleges of technology, 2) specialized training colleges(post-secondary courses), 3) junior colleges, 4) universities (undergraduate) and 5) graduate schools. […] Most higher educational institutions in Japan set their academic year from April to March of the following year. […] In Japan, most schools admit students in April, but some schools have an autumn admission system.
interpretation: Used for the shape of the sector and for the calendar, not for any deadline — this is a promotion agency and it may describe the system without being the final word on any rule inside it. Two things in it matter. The five-type list names the routes English-language guidance never mentions: the kōsen, which takes students at fifteen for a five-year technical programme, and the senmon gakkō, the professional training college, which is Japan's answer to the question this project asks of every country. And the calendar sentence is the one a European reader most needs: April is the default and autumn admission is the exception, which is why the small set of September-entry English-taught programmes exists at all.

claim: The University of Tokyo charges an admission fee of 282,000 yen once and annual undergraduate tuition of 642,960 yen, the same for every nationality. The page states no academic year and says nothing about the College of Design.
excerpt: Admission Fee: ¥282,000 [paid one time only at admission]. Tuition Fee: ¥642,960 [per year].
interpretation: Recorded with two warnings rather than as a clean figure. The admission fee of 282,000 yen is the national standard and has been for years; the tuition is not — the national standard is 535,800 yen and Todai has raised its own above it, which is precisely the reason not to quote a national figure for any particular Japanese university. The page carries no price year and says nothing about the new College of Design, whose five-year integrated programme may not be priced like an ordinary bachelor's. Japan charges the same to every nationality, so there is no EU/non-EU split to look for; the thing to budget separately for is the admission fee, which is charged once and is substantial.
